chunks: Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Abdullah ibn Ja'far al-Himyari, from Muhammad ibn al-Walid, who said: Al-Abbas ibn Hilal narrated to us from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him).

He said: 'Indeed, Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon him) said to him (Abu Hanifa): How do you rule with the oath alongside a single witness? Ja'far (peace be upon him) replied: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) ruled with it, and Ali (peace be upon him) ruled with it in your presence.' Abu Hanifa laughed, and Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'You rule with the testimony of one person as if it were the testimony of a hundred.' He asked: 'What do we do?' He replied: 'Yes, a hundred testify, and you send one to inquire about them, then you validate their testimony based on his statement.'

key_terms.أَبُو حَنِيفَةَ: Abu Hanifa (founder of the Hanafi school of jurisprudence)
key_terms.الْيَمِين: Oath (sworn statement used in legal testimony)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between the Ja'fari and Hanafi approaches to single-witness testimony and oaths?
ai.summary: This hadith highlights the jurisprudential divergence between the Ahl al-Bayt and the emerging Sunni schools regarding the weight of a single witness combined with an oath (yamin). Ja'far al-Sadiq critiques the Hanafi method of validating one witness through inquiry of others, arguing it artificially inflates the value of a single testimony, whereas the Shia tradition maintains the prophetic precedent of accepting a single witness with an oath as sufficient for judgment.
